planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Peppermint is grown for its distinctive two-tone raceme rather than the solid royal blue of common grape hyacinth.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light partial shade, spacing clusters closely for the densest color impact. Each raceme opens pale blue at the base with the florets fading progressively toward white at the crown, giving the spike a distinct banded, peppermint-like look rather than the uniform violet-blue of the species. The lightly fragrant flowers open in mid-spring and persist for several weeks, drawing early bees while the strappy foliage remains low and grassy. Established clumps naturalize readily and can be left undisturbed for years, dividing offset bulbs in summer dormancy only when clumps become congested.

common_name: Mount Hood Grape Hyacinth (White-Tipped Cobalt Blue Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; named for its snow-capped color pattern, Mount Hood naturalizes gently without becoming weedy.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun or light part shade, ideally in generous drifts of 25 or more for visual impact. Each dense, conical spike carries tubular florets that are cobalt blue through the base and middle of the raceme, sharply capped by pure white florets at the tip, producing a snow-capped effect distinct from the solid or gradient-blue tones of other aucheri selections. Bloom runs several weeks in mid to late spring, after which the narrow foliage yellows and should be left in place to recharge the bulb. Unlike common grape hyacinth, this compact selection stays well-behaved in beds, rock gardens, and containers rather than self-seeding aggressively.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to part shade; Superstar was selected for a softer periwinkle flower color rather than the royal blue of the wild species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to part shade, allowing clumps to build undisturbed for several seasons. Each scape carries a dense conical raceme of 20 to 40 fragrant, urn-shaped florets rimmed with a thin white edge, in a lighter periwinkle-blue that reads noticeably softer than the deep royal-blue of standard Armenian grape hyacinth. A single mature bulb can send up multiple scapes in a season, and the topmost florets remain sterile, serving mainly as a decorative crown above the fertile flowers below. Bloom occurs in early to mid spring and the deer-resistant bulbs naturalize freely in beds, borders, and lawns without special winter protection.

common_name: Gipsy Girl Crocus (Gold Snow Crocus with Purple-Brown Feathering)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; Gipsy Girl is one of the most heavily feathered of the chrysanthus snow crocus cultivars.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade, siting where late-winter sun can reach the emerging buds. The deep gold, goblet-shaped flowers are boldly marked on their outer petals with bronze-purple feathering that fades toward the base, a striking contrast that sets this selection apart from solid-colored chrysanthus cultivars. Like other snow crocus, the flowers open only in sunshine and close on cloudy days or after dusk, and blooming precedes most other spring bulbs by a week or two. Left undisturbed, corms multiply steadily by offsets and are well suited to naturalizing in short turf, rock gardens, or the front of a bulb border.

common_name: Advance Crocus (Lemon-Yellow Snow Crocus with Purple Flush)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Advance is valued for its unusual two-tone petals that read differently from the inside than the outside.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, grouping generously since individual flowers are small. Buds emerge with the outer petals flushed dusky purple and edged in white, opening to reveal a clear lemon-yellow interior with a violet-blue base and bright orange stamens, so the same flower shows two distinct color schemes depending on whether it is open or closed. Blooming in late winter to earliest spring, ahead of most other crocus, it tolerates a dry summer dormancy well and resents soggy soil during that rest period. This cultivar naturalizes reliably in rock gardens, gravel beds, and the edges of lawns where it can be left to multiply for years.

common_name: Prins Claus Crocus (White Snow Crocus with Purple-Violet Feathering)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; Prins Claus is a long-cultivated chrysanthus selection dating to the 1960s, still prized for its crisp white-and-purple contrast.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade for the cleanest color display. The outer three petals are rich purple-violet edged crisply in white, while the flower opens to a pure white interior centered on bright orange stamens, giving the small goblet-shaped bloom strong contrast from a distance. Flowers only fully unfurl in direct sun, closing tight on overcast days, and bloom arrives in late winter to earliest spring alongside other chrysanthus selections. Being compact, it suits window boxes and small containers as well as the front edge of a rock garden or bulb border, and corms multiply steadily without becoming invasive.
sources: Old House Gardens historic bulb reference

common_name: King of the Striped Crocus (Violet-Striped Dutch Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; King of the Striped is a long-lived, vigorous Dutch crocus grown for its bold striping rather than a solid flower color.

directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light shade, choosing a spot visible from a path or window since the striping is best appreciated up close. The large, goblet-shaped flowers are pale violet overlaid with bold, dark purple vertical stripes radiating from a deep purple base, opening to reveal a vivid orange center that contrasts sharply with the cool petal tones. Like other large-flowered Dutch crocus, blooms open widest in full sun and close during rain or at night, lasting about three weeks in early spring. This selection is notably vigorous and long-lived, readily naturalizing in turf or borders where it can be left undisturbed for decades.
sources: Brent and Becky's Bulbs plant reference

common_name: Firefly Crocus (Lilac-Pink Sieber's Crocus with Orange Throat)

planting.note: Plant corms about 3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; Firefly is among the earliest of all crocus to bloom, often opening through late snow cover.

directions: Plant corms about 3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a raised bed, trough, or rock garden pocket where drainage stays sharp year-round. Bicolor buds of orange-yellow and lavender open into soft lilac to pale violet flowers with a golden-orange throat at the base, a warmer color combination than the more uniformly blue-violet species form. Each narrow, dark green leaf carries a fine silvery central stripe, and the fragrant flowers appear in very late winter, among the first blooms of the gardening year alongside snowdrops. Left undisturbed, this alpine selection increases steadily by offsets and light self-seeding, gradually forming dense drifts over several seasons.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; Remembrance is a historic Dutch crocus selection dating to the early 1900s still valued for its glossy, uniform purple color.

directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light shade, siting in drifts along a border edge or lawn for a strong mass display. The large, chalice-shaped flowers are a rich violet-purple with a silvery sheen and a darker purple base, cupping bright yellow stamens toward the light as the petals open each morning. Grassy, narrow leaves marked with a thin silver band accompany the roughly three-week spring bloom before yellowing and dying back for summer dormancy. A long-lived heirloom selection, Remembrance persists for decades once established and multiplies steadily unless disturbed by digging rodents.
